topic: The Mathematical Foundations of Bitcoin: Trust through Cryptography
target_audience: University students with a basic interest in computer science

sections.title: Introduction: The Digital Ledger
sections.content: Define the problem of 'Double Spending' in digital currency and introduce the ledger as an immutable sequence of data blocks.
sections.example: Imagine a digital 'magic notebook' where Alice gives Bob a token; everyone in the room must agree that Alice had the token before the transaction is recorded.

sections.title: The Hash Function: The Digital Fingerprint
sections.content: Explain SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm). Focus on the 'one-way' property: it is easy to compute a fingerprint from data, but impossible to recreate data from the fingerprint.
sections.example: Visual: A blender turning a bowl of fruit (data) into a smoothie (hash). You can't turn the smoothie back into the original fruit.

sections.title: Proof of Work: The Mathematical Puzzle
sections.content: Introduce 'Mining' as finding a 'nonce' (number used once) that, when combined with transaction data, results in a hash starting with a specific number of zeros. This requires immense computational trial-and-error.
sections.example: Visual: A digital lottery where 1,000 robots are trying to guess a 6-digit combination. The first one to guess it gets to write the next page in the ledger.

sections.title: Public-Key Cryptography: Digital Signatures
sections.content: Prerequisite: Modulo arithmetic. Explain how users prove ownership using a Private Key (a secret number) and a Public Key (a derived coordinate on an Elliptic Curve).
sections.example: Visual: A 'lock and key' animation where Alice uses her private key to sign a transaction, and the network uses her public key to verify it without ever seeing the secret private key.

sections.title: Synthesis: Chain Integrity
sections.content: Explain how each block contains the hash of the previous block, creating an unbreakable chain. Changing one digit in block 1 changes its hash, breaking the link to all subsequent blocks.
sections.example: Visual: A row of falling dominoes. Each domino is etched with the 'fingerprint' of the one before it. If you move one, the whole sequence collapses and alerts the network.
